From cyberattacks to armed drones and mysterious cases of arson, tensions are rising across the continent as the war in Ukraine is set to enter its fifth winter. Just this month, Poland said it thwarted an attempted assassination of a U.S. citizen originally from Ukraine that was ordered by Russia while Estonia accused Moscow of being behind a fire at a drone maker. Meanwhile, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Tuesday that those responsible for hybrid attacks “will pay the price” after an explosive-laden drone was discovered at an airport in Leipzig near a Ukrainian cargo plane, raising speculation that Moscow was involved in an attempted strike. Amid an uptick in sabotage efforts, CIA Director John Ratcliffe traveled to Russia for meetings on Tuesday, according to people familiar with the matter. It was unclear what the talks were about. The Central Intelligence Agency declined to comment. Police investigators work on the tarmac with a robot that is capable, among other things, of defusing explosives, near to a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane Aug. 5 at Leipzig/Halle Airport near Leipzig, Germany. Jens Schlueter, Getty Images On Thursday, Russia warned that it could strike ​British military targets inside and outside Ukraine in response to Ukrainian attacks on targets inside Russia using long-range British ‌cruise missiles. European officials have been anticipating for months that Russia may escalate its aggressive campaign against the continent. But the bloc has yet to change its fundamentally defensive posture, according to people familiar with how the institutions gauge outside threats, who spoke on condition of anonymity. That has likely encouraged Moscow to probe how far it can go in trying to intimidate and wear down western allies as it remains locked in a war of attrition with Ukraine. “NATO, European and national responses have largely been reactive and defensive,” said Agnia Grigas, a non-resident fellow at the Atlantic Council in Vilnius. “They have focused on detecting and countering individual provocations, but have not built a record of effective deterrence by consistently dissuading Moscow from continuing or escalating them.” That lack of preparedness comes as Europe has taken on the primary role in supporting Ukraine with the U.S. shifting away from the continent. While NATO’s mutual defense clause commits member states to help each other in case of an attack, Russia’s alleged actions have so far fallen short of what would trigger such a response. Politics Ukrainian attacks on Wildberries warehouses strike at heart of Russia retail sector Reuters Moscow has increasingly relied on recruitment via social media to carry out arson or other sabotage attacks, after large-scale expulsions of its diplomats following the invasion of Ukraine. Two Ukrainian nationals were handed prison sentences in the U.K. in June, after a jury found them guilty of conspiring to commit arson attacks on a car and property linked to then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer. The prosecution said during the trial that one of the perpetrators was recruited online by a Russian-speaking Telegram user. Lithuanian Prosecutor General Nida Grunskiene said last week that the drone attack in Germany has “links” to an ongoing investigation into an attempt to detonate a parcel on a DHL cargo plane in 2024. Lithuania charged five in the attempted sabotage, allegedly hired by Russia’s military intelligence. While Germany hasn’t singled out Russia as being behind the armed drone, or the recent discovery of a cache of weapons on the outskirts of Berlin, a slew of investigative media reports pointed the finger at Moscow. It also added to fresh warnings that Europe’s biggest economy must grapple with the new dimensions of asymmetrical risks. Axel Schmidt, Reuters Russian hacker group Server Killers declared a cyber war against Norway in a post on Telegram over the country’s defense cooperation deal with Ukraine, broadcaster TV2 reported Tuesday. A number of Norway’s banking and government websites have been facing disruption from so-called distributed denial of service attacks since Monday, it said. There are indications that Russian intelligence and security services are looking at hybrid warfare operations against the Baltic States and Poland, an intelligence official told Bloomberg earlier this month. Lithuanian Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said Moscow is weighing a potential false flag operation using captured Ukrainian drones to strike critical infrastructure in the Baltic region. “Russia’s ongoing hybrid warfare in Europe is a highly coordinated, sub-threshold campaign aimed at destabilizing Western political systems, fracturing NATO and E.U. unity, and eroding support for Ukraine,” said Alex Kokcharov, geoeconomics analyst at Bloomberg Economics in London. “To achieve these goals, the Kremlin maintains plausible deniability by exploiting anonymity and utilizing proxies to obfuscate direct state attribution.” Some European Union members have called on the bloc to respond by adopting the sanctions that have been blocked including seizing assets, a ban on transporting Russian liquefied natural gas and restricting visas, according to people familiar with the matter. The E.U. is preparing another package of sanctions on hundreds of individuals and entities, which it aims to adopt in the fall, they said speaking on condition of anonymity. But as previous such measures have failed to restrain Moscow, it’s unlikely they will do so now. “Russia is willing to use kinetic means because until now they have been unsuccessful in discouraging support for Ukraine,” said Marek Kohv, head of the Security and Resilience program at the Tallinn-based International Centre for Defense and Security. “It is directly connected to how Russia is doing on the front line.” NATO members have pledged $80 billion in military aid to Ukraine for 2026 and “at least the equivalent levels” in 2027 at the alliance’s July summit in Ankara. The money is overwhelmingly coming from Europe. Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham greets staff during a visit Wednesday to a Sainsbury’s store in London. He also compared Ukraine’s fight to Britain’s resistance to the Nazis in World War II, drawing a response from Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov. He accused the U.K. of “methodically and regularly adding fuel to the fire” and “methodically and regularly plotting to prevent any progress in the peace process” in his remarks to reporters on Monday. Photograph: artaxerxes_longhand/Alamy Russia Russia arrests Japanese journalist on allegations of spying FSB security agency said reporter was arrested on island of Sakhalin, alleging he was collecting information about Russia’s defences Justin McCurry in Tokyo Tue 13 Oct 2026 21.05 EDT Last modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 22.44 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Russia has arrested a Japanese journalist on the far east island of Sakhalin and accused him of spying, in the latest sign of rising tensions between Moscow and Tokyo. Russian foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova identified the reporter as Yuki Imai, from the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, adding that he had been accused of “conducting espionage activities on Russian territory”. Imai, a reporter at the newspaper’s bureau in the city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk on Sakhalin, was reportedly preparing to return to Japan when he was arrested for allegedly collecting information on Russia’s defence capabilities, according to Russia’s Tass news agency. Russia’s FSB security agency claimed the journalist had intended to pass the information on to Japanese intelligence. The FSB published a video showing masked officers storming a hotel room, pushing a man to the floor and handcuffing him. The man was flown to Moscow, where a court ordered he be held in pre-trial detention. It did not say when the arrest or court hearing occurred. The charges carry up to 20 years in prison. Japan’s foreign ministry urged Moscow to extend “fair and impartial treatment” to the detained journalist. “The Japanese embassy … in Moscow and the consulate general in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk lodged a request with the Russian authorities for the prompt provision of information, as well as for humanitarian consideration and fair and impartial treatment,” an official told Agence France-Presse. The Hokkaido Shimbun said in a statement that it was aware of the announcement by Russian authorities but it was “still confirming the details”. “Ensuring the safety of the journalist is our top priority, and we are responding accordingly,” it said. Imai’s arrest comes amid rapidly deteriorating ties between Japan and Russia, triggered by Tokyo’s support for Ukraine and a longstanding dispute over sovereignty of islands belonging to the Kuril chain near Sakhalin that are known in Japan as the Northern Territories. Japan claims the four islands closest to its territory – the nearest is less than 4km from Hokkaido. Russia regards Japan as an “unfriendly” country because it has joined western sanctions over its war ⁠in Ukraine. Russia has arrested several citizens of “unfriendly” countries in recent years, accusing them of working for western intelligence services. In 2023, US journalist Evan Gershkovich was arrested on espionage charges, later sentenced to 16 years in prison before being released in a 2024 prisoner swap . The Kuril Islands: how a visit from Putin reignited a 150-year-old dispute between Japan and Russia Read more The FSB said it had “opened a criminal case against the Japanese national”, and that he had been placed in pre-trial detention, Russian news agencies reported, citing the agency. Russian media reported he would remain in custody until 12 December. “Attempts by Tokyo to use its correspondents in Russia … to gather information aimed at undermining the security of our state is regrettable,” Zakharova said, alleging this was “not an isolated case”. The Kurils have been under Russian control since the end of the second world war, when Soviet forces seized the islands in the final days of the conflict, forcing about 17,000 Japanese citizens to leave and, over time, replacing them with a similar number of Russians. In 2022, Moscow scrapped a programme that allowed former residents to travel to the islands to visit the graves of their ancestors in protest at Japan’s support for Ukraine. Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, visited one of the disputed islands in August, causing an ​uproar in Japan . Tokyo has ‌said it would continue ​implementing sanctions against ​Russia and supporting Ukraine.
